name: Identify objects in the sky and space
description: Student can name common objects seen in the sky and in space, including the sun, moon, stars and planets, when shown pictures of them or asked to point them out.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown picture cards (sun, moon, a star, a planet, a cloud, a bird), the student picks out the sun, moon, star and planet and names each one.
commonError: Student groups everything in the sky together as 'stars', or calls the moon a planet.
checkpointTask: Show four or five picture cards of sky and space objects mixed with non-examples (cloud, bird, plane). Ask the student to name each space object.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Foundational identification IC, directly from elaboration 1. No scaffold removal.

name: Describe Earth's shape from space images
description: Student can describe the shape of Earth as round, like a ball or sphere, using photographs or video of Earth taken from space.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown a photo of Earth from space, the student says Earth is round or ball-shaped, not flat.
commonError: Student describes Earth as flat based on everyday experience of the ground, or confuses a photo of Earth with the moon.
checkpointTask: Show two or three real images of Earth from space. Ask the student what shape Earth is and how they can tell.
reviewNotes: Confidence MEDIUM. Scope-edge IC: 'shape of Earth' comes from an elaboration and underpins 'Earth is a planet', but is not in the descriptor text or the achievement standard. Candidate to cut if you want a tighter set. Your call.

name: Identify Earth as a planet in the solar system
description: Student can point to or name Earth as one of the planets when shown a model, diagram or picture of the solar system.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a labelled solar system poster, the student points to Earth, says it is the planet we live on, and recognises it as one of several planets near the sun.
commonError: Student thinks Earth is the centre of the solar system, or does not recognise Earth as a planet because it looks different from the others in diagrams.
checkpointTask: Show a simple solar system diagram. Ask the student to find Earth and say what kind of object it is.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Core knowledge for the first clause of the descriptor. No scaffold removal.

name: Sort sky objects by day or night
description: Student can sort sky objects and sights by whether they are usually seen during the day or during the night.
exampleOfSuccess: Given cards for the sun, stars, a bright moon and a blue daytime sky, the student places the sun and blue sky under 'day' and stars under 'night', and notes the moon can sometimes be seen in both.
commonError: Student assumes the moon is only ever a night-time object, or that stars disappear during the day rather than just being not visible.
checkpointTask: Give the student picture cards of sky sights and two hoops labelled day and night. Ask them to sort and explain one choice.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the day/night visibility elaboration. The moon-in-both nuance in the example is a stretch, not required for a pass.

name: Describe the sun's path across a day
description: Student can describe how the sun appears to move across the sky during a day, from one side in the morning to high near the middle of the day to the other side in the afternoon, based on their own observation or a time-lapse rather than on being told the rule.
exampleOfSuccess: After tracking the sun at three points in a day or watching a time-lapse, the student describes the sun as low on one side in the morning, high at lunchtime, and low on the other side later.
commonError: Student says the sun 'moves' without describing a pattern, or describes the sun travelling around a still sky rather than its apparent path.
checkpointTask: Show a time-lapse of the sun across a day, or three photos taken morning, midday and afternoon. Ask the student to describe how the sun's position changed.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Scaffold note: description specifies 'from observation or time-lapse, not from being told the rule' to separate genuine pattern observation from recall. Ceiling held at 'describe the apparent path', not 'explain why', per the achievement standard.

name: Describe the pattern in changing shadows
description: Student can observe that shadows change in a regular way as the sun's position changes through the day, and describe that pattern.
exampleOfSuccess: After marking a fixed object's shadow at three times in a day, the student says the shadow was long in the morning, shortest near midday, and long again later, and links this to where the sun was.
commonError: Student notices the shadow changed but cannot link it to the sun's position, or expects the shadow to point the same way all day.
checkpointTask: Mark a fixed object's shadow at two or three times in a day, or show prepared photos. Ask the student to describe how and why the shadow changed.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the shadow-length elaboration. Kept 'length' as the core observable and put direction in the example to avoid bundling two distinct observables into one IC.

name: Record the moon's pattern of change
description: Student can record the moon's shape across several observations over weeks (a moon diary) and describe the repeating pattern in how the shape changes.
exampleOfSuccess: Using a class moon diary, the student describes the moon going from a thin sliver to a full round shape and back, and notes that this keeps repeating.
commonError: Student records shapes but treats each as a one-off rather than a repeating cycle, or expects the moon to change shape within a single night.
checkpointTask: Show a completed moon diary or a sequence of moon images across a month. Ask the student to describe the pattern in the moon's changing shape.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the moon-diary elaboration. Depends on data gathered over time, so the checkpoint offers a prepared diary as an alternative to a month-long wait.

name: Predict from an observed sky pattern
description: Student can use a sky pattern they have already observed, such as the moon's sequence of shapes or the sun's daily path, to predict what will happen next.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a moon diary showing the moon getting fuller each night, the student predicts it will be full or nearly full in a few nights and gives the pattern as the reason.
commonError: Student guesses without using the pattern, or predicts a change that breaks the observed cycle.
checkpointTask: Show part of a sky pattern (a few days of moon shapes, or the sun's morning and midday positions). Ask the student to predict what comes next and why.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. CROSS-DESCRIPTOR CANDIDATE: strongly underpins AC9S2I01 and AC9S2H01. NOT auto-linked: flagging for you to decide on linkedDescriptorIds.

name: Tell regular sky events from irregular ones
description: Student can decide whether a given sky event is a regular, repeating event (such as a full moon each month or the sun rising each day) or an irregular, rare event (such as a 'blood' or 'blue' moon).
exampleOfSuccess: Given examples, the student sorts 'full moon', 'sunrise' and 'phases of the moon' as regular, and 'blood moon' and 'eclipse' as rare or irregular.
commonError: Student treats anything unfamiliar as irregular, or assumes a rare-sounding name like 'blood moon' means the event never repeats.
checkpointTask: Name or show four or five sky events. Ask the student to sort each as regular and repeating or rare and irregular.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium-high. From the regular-vs-irregular elaboration. Kept at 'identify/sort' level; reasoning about why an event is rare exceeds the Year 2 ceiling.

name: First Nations sky pattern knowledge
description: Student can describe one example of how First Nations Peoples of Australia use patterns in the sky, such as star or moon patterns, to mark seasons, events or directions.
exampleOfSuccess: After hearing or reading a First Nations account, the student explains that a particular star pattern appearing signals a season or a time to act, such as when certain foods become available.
commonError: Student retells the account as a story only, without connecting it to a real observed sky pattern or its practical use.
checkpointTask: Share an age-appropriate First Nations account of a sky pattern. Ask the student to describe the sky pattern and what it was used to know or predict.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium, OPTIONAL. RECOMMEND sourcing from a First Nations authored or endorsed resource.

name: Make sounds using different actions
description: Student can make a sound from an object using a chosen action such as striking, blowing, scraping, plucking or shaking, and name the action used.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a drum, a recorder, a scraper and a rubber band on a box, the student makes a sound from each and says whether they struck, blew, scraped or plucked it.
commonError: Student makes sounds but cannot name or distinguish the action, or thinks only instruments can make sound.
checkpointTask: Put out four or five everyday objects. Ask the student to make a sound from each and name the action used.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From elaboration 2. Foundational doing-and-naming IC.

name: Describe a sound as loud or soft
description: Student can describe a sound they hear or make as loud or soft.
exampleOfSuccess: After tapping a drum gently then hard, the student says the first was soft and the second was loud.
commonError: Student confuses loudness with pitch, calling a high sound 'loud' or a low sound 'soft'.
checkpointTask: Make pairs of sounds that differ only in loudness. Ask the student which is loud and which is soft.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Loudness vocabulary from elaboration 1. Deliberately separated from pitch to keep one attribute per IC.

name: Describe a sound as high or low
description: Student can describe a sound they hear or make as high or low in pitch.
exampleOfSuccess: Played a high note and a low note on a xylophone, the student identifies which is high and which is low.
commonError: Student maps 'high' to loud and 'low' to soft, confusing pitch with loudness.
checkpointTask: Play pairs of sounds that differ only in pitch. Ask the student which is higher.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Pitch vocabulary from elaboration 1.

name: Change an action to change a sound
description: Student can change one thing about how a sound is made, such as how hard they strike or how a ruler is held over a desk edge, to make the sound different, and describe what they changed.
exampleOfSuccess: Twanging a ruler over the desk edge, the student moves more of the ruler off the edge, says the sound got lower, and names what they changed.
commonError: Student changes the sound but cannot say what they did differently, or changes two things at once so the cause is unclear.
checkpointTask: Give the student a ruler on a desk or a stretched rubber band. Ask them to make the sound change and tell you the one thing they changed.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the twanged-ruler elaboration 5.

name: Recognise objects vibrate when making sound
description: Student can show or point to the back-and-forth movement (vibration) that happens when an object makes a sound, such as a twanged ruler, a tuning fork or a speaker.
exampleOfSuccess: Holding a sounding tuning fork to the surface of water, the student points to the splashing and says the fork is moving quickly back and forth.
commonError: Student thinks the sound and the movement are unrelated, or cannot detect the vibration when it is too small to see easily.
checkpointTask: Provide a tuning fork and water, a twanged ruler, or a speaker with a light object on it. Ask the student to find and describe the movement that goes with the sound.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Core vibration concept from elaborations 5 and 6.

name: Observe that bigger vibrations make louder sounds
description: Student can observe that making an object vibrate more strongly produces a louder sound, and describe the link between the size of the vibration and the loudness.
exampleOfSuccess: Twanging a ruler gently then harder, the student notes the bigger movement made the louder sound.
commonError: Student expects a bigger vibration to change the pitch rather than the loudness, or does not connect vibration size to loudness at all.
checkpointTask: Ask the student to make the same object give a soft then a loud sound, and to tell you what was different about the movement each time.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium-high. Sits at the top of the Year 2 ceiling.

name: Identify materials that muffle sound
description: Student can compare materials and identify which ones make a sound quieter when placed around or over the sound source.
exampleOfSuccess: Wrapping a ticking timer in cloth, then foil, then leaving it bare, the student says the cloth made it quietest.
commonError: Student judges by how thick a material looks rather than by listening, or changes more than one thing between tries.
checkpointTask: Give the student a sound source and two or three materials. Ask them to find which material muffles the sound most, listening each time.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium. Borderline with Science Inquiry Skills. Candidate to move or cut. Your call.

name: First Nations instruments and their sounds
description: Student can describe how a traditional musical instrument used by First Nations Australians makes its characteristic sound, such as the action that sets it vibrating.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown or hearing a clapstick or didgeridoo, the student says how the sound is made (striking or blowing) and that the instrument vibrates.
commonError: Student describes the instrument's appearance or use only, without connecting to how the sound is produced.
checkpointTask: Share an age-appropriate resource on a First Nations instrument. Ask the student how its sound is made.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium, OPTIONAL. RECOMMEND a First Nations authored or endorsed resource.

name: Physically change a material with an action
description: Student can change the shape or form of a material using an action such as bending, twisting, stretching, scrunching, folding, tearing or cutting, and name the action used.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a sheet of paper, the student folds it, tears it and scrunches it, naming each action.
commonError: Student thinks a material has only one fixed form, or cannot name the action that produced the change.
checkpointTask: Give the student paper or fabric. Ask them to change it in three different ways and name each action.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From elaborations 1 and 2.

name: Choose an action for a wanted change
description: Student can choose a suitable action to make a wanted physical change to a material, such as tearing or cutting to make it smaller, or bending to change its shape.
exampleOfSuccess: Asked to make a strip of paper shorter without tools, the student tears it; asked to make it curl, the student rolls or bends it.
commonError: Student picks an action that does not achieve the goal, or assumes a tool is always needed.
checkpointTask: Name two or three wanted changes (smaller, curved, longer). Ask the student which action they would use for each.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium. Lean-cut candidate if you want a tighter set.

name: Recognise the material stays the same
description: Student can recognise that after a physical change, such as folding paper or crushing chalk into powder, the material is still the same material.
exampleOfSuccess: After crushing chalk to powder, the student says it is still chalk even though it looks different.
commonError: Student thinks a big change in appearance (chalk to powder, paper torn to bits) means it has become a different material.
checkpointTask: Physically change a material in front of the student (crush chalk, tear paper). Ask whether it is still the same material and how they know.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Core concept of the descriptor and achievement standard.

name: Compare a property before and after
description: Student can compare one property of a material, such as size, shape or texture, before and after a physical change.
exampleOfSuccess: Comparing a stick of chalk with the powder it became, the student says the powder is in tiny pieces and feels different, but is the same colour.
commonError: Student lists changes without comparing to the original state, or assumes every property changed when only some did.
checkpointTask: Show a material before and after a physical change. Ask the student what stayed the same and what is different.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the chalk elaboration 3.

name: Spot the different material (odd one out)
description: Student can identify which sample is a different material when shown several samples of the same material that has been physically changed in different ways.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown torn, folded and scrunched paper plus one piece of fabric, the student picks the fabric as the odd one out and explains the others are all paper.
commonError: Student picks the most differently shaped sample as the odd one out rather than the one that is a different material.
checkpointTask: Lay out three or four physically changed samples of one material and one sample of a different material. Ask the student to find the odd one out and say why.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. From the 'odd one out' elaboration 5.

name: Change a material to suit a purpose
description: Student can physically change a material to make it better suited to a purpose, and say how the change helped.
exampleOfSuccess: Twisting several strands of wool together, the student makes a stronger thread and explains the twisting made it harder to break.
commonError: Student makes a change that does not serve the purpose, or cannot explain how the change helped.
checkpointTask: Set a simple purpose (paper that flies further, thread that is stronger). Ask the student to change the material to suit it and explain their choice.
reviewNotes: Confidence high. Application IC from elaboration 1.

name: First Nations physical changes to materials
description: Student can describe how First Nations Australians physically change a natural material to make a useful object, such as shaping fibres into a basket or bowl.
exampleOfSuccess: Shown how plant fibres are twisted and woven into a basket, the student describes the physical changes (twisting, weaving) and that the fibre is still fibre.
commonError: Student focuses on the finished object only, without identifying the physical changes made or that the material is unchanged in kind.
checkpointTask: Share an age-appropriate resource on a First Nations fibre craft or tool. Ask the student what physical changes were made to the material.
reviewNotes: Confidence medium, OPTIONAL. RECOMMEND a First Nations authored or endorsed resource.
